lessons.title: Understanding Forge Types: Coal, Gas, and Propane
lessons.body:
A forge is simply a controlled fire that gets hot enough to make metal soft. In Africa, the most common forge is a coal forge, often made from a car wheel rim, a metal bucket, or a simple clay mound. Coal forges burn charcoal or mineral coal. Charcoal is made by burning wood slowly with little air; it lights easily and is cheap, but burns fast. Mineral coal burns hotter and longer but needs a good air blast from a hand-cranked blower or electric fan. A coal forge needs a firepot (a shallow bowl) and a tuyere (a pipe that brings air into the fire). You can build one from scrap: a brake drum works well as a firepot, and a length of pipe with a hair dryer or hand blower provides air.

Gas forges run on propane or butane. They are cleaner and easier to light, but the fuel must be bought. A basic gas forge is a metal drum or pipe lined with ceramic fibre or firebrick to hold heat. A burner (often a simple pipe with a small hole for air) mixes gas and air, and the flame swirls inside the chamber. Gas forges heat metal without smoke or ash, so they are good in towns where coal smoke is a problem. However, they can be more expensive to run and require a steady supply of gas cylinders.

Propane is the same as cooking gas in many countries. A 9 kg cylinder will run a small forge for about 8 to 10 hours. You need a regulator and a hose rated for gas. Never use a homemade regulator or a leaking hose. Gas forges must have a way for exhaust gases to escape, or you risk carbon monoxide poisoning. Always work outdoors or in a well-ventilated shed.

Choose your forge based on what you have. If you have scrap metal and wood to make charcoal, build a coal forge. If you live in a city with gas supply, a gas forge may be easier. Many smiths start with coal and later add a gas forge for smaller jobs. The key is to learn to control the fire, no matter what fuel you use.

lessons.title: Building and Maintaining a Coal Fire
lessons.body:
To build a coal fire, start with a clean firepot. Remove old clinker (the glassy waste that blocks air) and ash. Place a handful of dry kindling or paper in the bottom, then add small pieces of charcoal or coal. Light the kindling from the top, and turn on the air blast gently. As the fire catches, add more coal around the edges, leaving a hollow in the centre. This hollow is where you will put your metal. The fire should be bright orange-yellow, not dull red.

Once the fire is going, you need to keep it fed. Add coal little by little around the outside, not directly on the hot centre. Green coal (new coal) smokes and gives off yellow smoke, which is normal. As it heats, it turns to coke and burns clean. Use a poker to break up clinker and keep air passages open. The fire should be about the size of a melon for most work. If you need a bigger fire, add more coal and increase air. If the fire gets too big, stop adding coal and let it burn down.

Maintaining the fire means watching the colour. A good forging fire is bright yellow-orange. If it is dark red, you need more air. If it is white and sparking, it is too hot and you are burning the metal. The metal should be placed in the fire at the same depth each time, usually about 2-3 cm below the surface of the coal. Rotate the metal so it heats evenly. Never leave metal in the fire while you do other tasks; it can burn.

In Africa, many smiths use charcoal instead of coal. Charcoal burns faster, so you need to add it more often. A charcoal fire is ready when the coals are glowing red with a little ash on top. You can use a hand-powered bellows made from a plastic bag or a wooden box to provide air. Keep the bellows or blower working steadily; too much air blows ash into the metal, too little makes a cold fire. After work, let the fire die down, then clean out the firepot and dispose of ash safely.

lessons.title: Controlling Fire Temperature and Size
lessons.body:
Controlling the fire is the most important skill in blacksmithing. Temperature is controlled by the amount of air you blow into the fire and the amount of fuel. More air means more oxygen, which makes the fire hotter. But too much air can burn the metal or blow sparks. For most forging, you want a bright orange heat, around 1,100 to 1,200 degrees Celsius. That is hot enough to make steel soft like clay. If you need to weld, you need a white heat, around 1,300 degrees Celsius. You can judge temperature by colour: dark red is about 600Â°C, bright red 900Â°C, orange 1,100Â°C, yellow 1,200Â°C, white 1,300Â°C.

To increase temperature, add more air by turning up the blower or pumping the bellows faster. You can also add more coal around the centre. To decrease temperature, reduce air or spread the coal out. The size of the fire also matters. A small fire concentrates heat, good for small parts like hooks. A large fire spreads heat, good for long pieces like tongs. You can shape the fire by piling coal into a mound for a small hot spot, or spreading it flat for a wide heat.

Use a damper or a valve on your air supply to make fine adjustments. If you have an electric blower, a simple switch or a speed control works. With a hand-cranked blower, you control speed by how fast you turn. Always keep a bucket of water nearby to cool the fire if it gets too hot. You can also sprinkle water on the coal around the edge to keep it from burning too fast.

Practice by heating a piece of scrap steel. Watch the colour change as you increase air. Learn to hold a steady heat. In Africa, where fuel may be scarce, controlling the fire also saves money. A well-controlled fire uses less coal or charcoal. Remember, a forge fire is like a living thing: it needs food (fuel), air, and attention. With practice, you will know exactly how much air and fuel to use for each job.

lessons.title: Using a Gas Forge: Setup and Adjustment
lessons.body:
A gas forge is simpler to light than a coal forge, but you must set it up safely. First, place the forge on a stable, fireproof surface like concrete or bare earth. Never put it on wood or near flammable materials. Connect the gas hose to the burner and the regulator to the gas cylinder. Use soapy water to check for leaks: if bubbles form, tighten the connection. Open the cylinder valve slowly. Then open the burner valve a little and light the burner with a long match or spark lighter. Never lean over the forge when lighting; keep your face and hands to the side.

Once lit, adjust the air intake on the burner. Most burners have a sliding sleeve that controls air. If the flame is yellow and lazy, it needs more air. If it is blue and roaring, it is good. A proper flame is blue with a slight roar. If the flame blows out, turn off the gas, wait a minute, and try again with less gas. The forge chamber should heat up to orange in about 5 minutes. You can adjust the gas flow with the regulator or a needle valve. More gas means more heat, but also more fuel use.

To control temperature, you can adjust the gas and air. For most forging, you want the inside of the forge to be bright orange. If it is too hot, the metal will sparkle and burn. If too cold, the metal will not soften. You can also use a firebrick to block part of the opening to keep heat in. A gas forge is best for small to medium pieces. For long pieces, you may need to open both ends or use a larger forge.

In Africa, propane is available in many towns, but it can be expensive. A 9 kg cylinder lasts about 8 hours at full blast. To save gas, turn down the burner when you are not heating metal. Always turn off the gas at the cylinder when finished. Let the forge cool before moving it. Check the hose and regulator regularly for cracks. Never use a gas forge indoors without proper ventilation. Carbon monoxide is invisible and deadly.

lessons.title: Fire Safety and Emergency Procedures
lessons.body:
Fire safety starts before you light the forge. Clear the area around your forge of dry grass, paper, rags, and any flammable liquids. Keep a bucket of water, a bucket of sand, and a fire extinguisher within arm's reach. In Africa, many workshops are outdoors or in open sheds, so wind can carry sparks. Work with your back to the wind if possible, and never light a forge near thatched roofs or fuel stores. Wear cotton or leather clothing, not synthetic, because synthetic melts and sticks to skin. Leather boots, gloves, and safety glasses are essential.

When lighting a coal forge, use dry kindling and never use petrol or paraffin to start the fire. That is a common and deadly mistake. If the fire gets out of control, do not panic. Turn off the air blast first. That will cool the fire quickly. Then spread the coals with a rake or shovel. If flames spread to nearby materials, use the water or sand. For a gas forge, if you smell gas, turn off the cylinder immediately. Do not light a match or switch on a light. Open all doors and windows. If the gas has been leaking, let it air out before trying to light.

Burns are the most common injury. For a minor burn, cool it with clean running water for 10 minutes, then cover with a clean cloth. Do not use butter or oil. For a serious burn, get medical help. If you get metal in your eye, do not rub it. Cover the eye and go to a clinic. Always keep a first aid kit with bandages, antiseptic, and burn gel.

Emergency procedures: know where the nearest water tap and phone are. If a fire starts, call for help. If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop, and roll. Never run. In case of a gas leak, evacuate the area and call the fire service. Practice your emergency plan with everyone in the workshop. A few minutes of preparation can save lives and property.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Maintaining Your Forge
lessons.body:
After every forging session, clean your forge. For a coal forge, let the fire die out completely. Do not pour water on a hot firepot; it can crack cast iron. Once cool, remove ash and clinker with a small shovel or spoon. Clinker is the glassy, rock-like waste that forms from impurities in coal. If left, it blocks air and makes the fire burn poorly. Dump ash in a metal container, not a plastic bin, because ash can stay hot for hours. Scrape the firepot clean and check the tuyere for blockages. A wire brush works well.

For a gas forge, turn off the gas at the cylinder and let the forge cool. Remove any scale or flux that has dripped onto the floor of the forge. A stiff wire brush or a scraper will do. Check the ceramic fibre lining for cracks. Small cracks are normal, but large ones let heat escape and can cause hot spots. You can patch small cracks with refractory cement. Check the burner tube for spider webs or dirt; a pipe cleaner or compressed air can clear it. Inspect the hose and regulator for cracks or wear. Replace any damaged parts immediately.

Maintain your air supply. For a hand-cranked blower, oil the bearings regularly. For an electric blower, clean the fan blades and check the wiring. A clogged blower reduces air and makes the fire cold. Keep the blower dry. For a bellows, check for holes in the leather or plastic; patch them with tape or glue. Store your forge under cover if possible. Moisture rusts metal parts. If you live in a humid area, wipe metal surfaces with an oily rag.

A well-maintained forge lasts for years and works better. Keep a log of any repairs or parts you replace. In Africa, where parts may be hard to find, improvise with local materials: a car brake drum for a firepot, a metal pipe for a tuyere, a plastic bag for bellows. But always prioritise safety. A clean forge is a safe forge. Spend ten minutes after each session to clean and check your equipment. It will save you time and money in the long run.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: The Forge and Fire Management for African Blacksmiths

In African blacksmithing, the forge is not simply a tool â it is the heart of the workshop, the difference between a profitable day and a wasted one. Whether you are forging pangas in Tanzania, hoes in Malawi, knives in Ghana, or door hinges in Nigeria, your ability to build, control, and maintain fire determines your output quality, your fuel costs, and your safety. This practical reference gives you the technical knowledge to run a forge that earns money.

For small-scale African smiths, the forge often represents the single largest recurring cost after labour. Charcoal prices in urban and peri-urban areas have risen sharply â in many East African cities, a sack of charcoal that cost the equivalent of $8 in 2015 now costs $15â$20. Gas forges, while cleaner and faster, require upfront investment and reliable gas supply. Understanding your options is a business decision, not just a technical one.

Understanding Forge Types: Coal, Gas, and Propane

African smiths typically work with three forge types: traditional charcoal/coal forges (often clay-lined or metal drum forges), gas forges using LPG or propane, and hybrid setups. Each has distinct cost, performance, and context profiles.

Table 1: Forge Type Comparison for African Small-Scale Operations
Forge Type Fuel Source Typical Operating Cost (USD/hour) Heat Range (Â°C) Best For Key Limitation
Traditional Charcoal Forge Wood charcoal / lump charcoal $0.80 â $2.00 900 â 1,250 General blacksmithing, low capital High smoke, slow heat-up, fuel price volatility
Coal Forge (Bituminous) Bituminous coal / coke $0.60 â $1.50 1,100 â 1,400 Welding, heavy forging Smoke and sulphur emissions, clinker management
Gas Forge (LPG/Propane) LPG cylinder or propane tank $1.50 â $4.00 1,100 â 1,350 Clean work, knives, small items Upfront cost, gas refill logistics, cylinder safety
Hybrid (Coal + Gas) Coal primary, gas back-up $1.00 â $2.50 1,000 â 1,350 Flexible workshops Higher equipment investment

Sources: Adapted from Practical Action, Blacksmithing for Rural Development (2019); FAO, Small-Scale Metalworking in Africa (2017); field data from Kenyan and Tanzanian artisan workshops (2022).

Building and Maintaining a Coal Fire

A properly built coal fire is the foundation of efficient forging. The goal is a deep, concentrated fire with a clean, hot centre â not a wide, shallow fire that wastes fuel and produces inconsistent heat.

Step-by-step fire building:

  1. Clear the fire pot of old clinker and ash. A clean pot ensures proper airflow.
  2. Place a small amount of paper or dry kindling at the bottom of the pot, directly above the tuyere.
  3. Cover with a handful of dry wood shavings or small sticks. Light the kindling.
  4. Once the wood is burning well, add a small amount of coal around the edges of the fire â not on top. This allows the coal to coke (release volatiles) before reaching the hot centre.
  5. Gradually push coked coal toward the centre as it ignites. Add more coal around the perimeter and repeat.
  6. Maintain a fire that is roughly the size of a football (soccer ball) for general work. For welding, build a deeper, narrower fire.

Maintenance tips for African workshops:

  • Manage clinker: Impurities in coal melt into clinker â a glassy, solid mass that blocks airflow. Remove clinker every 30â45 minutes by lifting it out with a poker. In areas where coal quality is poor (common in parts of West Africa), clinker management is critical.
  • Water management: A light sprinkle of water around the fire's edge helps control the fire size and reduces dust. Do not soak the fire.
  • Fuel economy: Never let the fire burn wide and lazy. A focused fire uses 30â40% less fuel than a sprawling one. This directly affects your profit margin.

Controlling Fire Temperature and Size

Temperature control is the skill that separates a competent smith from a master. Different operations require different heats:

Table 2: Forging Temperatures and Fire Management by Operation
Operation Temperature Range (Â°C) Colour Indicator Fire Size Air Management
Forging (general shaping) 850 â 1,100 Cherry red to orange Medium (football size) Moderate, steady blast
Welding (forge welding) 1,200 â 1,350 Bright yellow to white Deep, narrow fire Strong, focused blast
Bending / twisting 700 â 950 Dark red to cherry red Medium Light to moderate blast
Annealing / normalising 750 â 900 Dull red to cherry red Large, even fire Low blast, even heat
Tempering (edge tools) 200 â 350 Straw to blue (oxide colours) Small, controlled fire Very low, indirect heat

Sources: Adapted from FAO, Small-Scale Metalworking in Africa (2017); British Artist Blacksmiths Association, Forge Temperature Guide (2021); field verification with Kenyan smiths, 2023.

Practical control levers:

  • Air blast: More air = hotter fire, but too much air wastes fuel and can burn steel. Use a hand-crank blower, bellows, or electric fan with a damper.
  • Fuel depth: A deeper fire concentrates heat. A shallow fire spreads it.
  • Fuel type: Coke burns hotter and cleaner than raw coal. If you can source coke, use it for welding and high-temperature work.
  • Workpiece placement: Place the workpiece in the hottest zone â just above the tuyere, buried in the fire. Do not lay it on top of the fire.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â FIRE AND BURN HAZARDS

Never leave a lit forge unattended. Always have a bucket of water or sand within arm's reach. Wear leather gloves, eye protection, and closed leather boots â not sandals. In many African workshops, open footwear and loose clothing are common causes of severe burns. Ensure adequate ventilation: coal and charcoal fires produce carbon monoxide, a colourless, odourless gas that can kill in enclosed spaces. If you feel dizzy, headache, or nausea, move to fresh air immediately and seek help. Gas forges: check all connections with soapy water before lighting. Never use a gas forge in a confined space without ventilation. Store LPG cylinders upright, outside, away from heat sources.

Using a Gas Forge: Setup and Adjustment

Gas forges are increasingly popular among African smiths producing high-value items â knives, tools, decorative pieces â because they are clean, fast, and do not require coal sourcing. However, they demand disciplined setup and safety.

Setup checklist:

  • Place the forge on a stable, non-flammable surface (concrete, stone, or earth â not wood).
  • Connect the gas hose to the regulator and burner. Check for leaks with soapy water.
  • Open the forge door or ensure ventilation before lighting.
  • Light a match or torch, hold it at the burner opening, then slowly open the gas valve.
  • Adjust the air choke and gas flow to achieve a neutral flame â a steady blue flame with a slight roar.
  • Allow the forge to reach temperature (5â10 minutes) before inserting work.

Adjustment for different tasks: For welding, increase gas and air for a hotter flame. For tempering, reduce gas and use a lower, softer flame. Always adjust gradually and observe the workpiece colour.

Cleaning and Maintaining Your Forge

Maintenance is not optional â it is a business investment. A well-maintained forge lasts years; a neglected one costs you fuel, time, and safety.

  • After every session: Remove ash and clinker. Wipe down the forge body. Check the tuyere for blockages.
  • Weekly: Inspect the clay lining for cracks. Repair with fire clay or a clay-sand mixture. Check the air supply system (bellows, blower, or fan) for wear.
  • Monthly: Deep-clean the fire pot. Check gas hoses and connections for cracks or leaks. Inspect the forge structure for heat damage.
  • Seasonally: Re-line the fire pot if the clay is significantly degraded. Replace worn tuyere pipes. Service blowers or fans.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Fire pot cleared of clinker and ash before lighting
  • â Fire built with kindling at bottom, coal added around edges first
  • â Air blast adjusted for task (moderate for forging, strong for welding)
  • â Workpiece placed in hottest zone, not on top of fire
  • â Water bucket or sand within arm's reach at all times
  • â PPE worn: leather gloves, eye protection, closed boots
  • â Ventilation adequate â no enclosed spaces with coal/gas fires
  • â Forge cleaned and inspected after every session

Further Reading

  • Practical Action â Blacksmithing and Metalworking Resources (free technical briefs on forge construction and fuel efficiency)
  • FAO â Small-Scale Metalworking in Africa (free PDF on appropriate technology and rural enterprise)
  • UK Health and Safety Executive â Welding and Forge Safety (free guidance applicable to workshop safety)
  • Anvilfire â Blacksmithing Reference and Forge Management (free articles on fire control and forge types)
  • I Forge Iron â Community Forum and Tutorials (free discussions on coal and gas forge setup)

Business note: In the African context, your forge is a production asset. Track your fuel consumption per item produced. If you make 10 hoes per day and use $6 of charcoal, your fuel cost per hoe is $0.60. If you can reduce that to $0.40 through better fire management, you add $2 per day to your margin â over a year, that is over $700. Fire management is profit management.

quiz.q: What is the most common material for a coal forge firepot in Africa?
options: A) A car wheel rim or brake drum
quiz.explanation: Car wheel rims and brake drums are commonly used because they are durable and easily available as scrap.

quiz.q: Which fuel burns hotter and longer in a coal forge?
quiz.explanation: Mineral coal has a higher energy density and burns longer than charcoal.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a tuyere in a coal forge?
options: B) To bring air into the fire
quiz.explanation: The tuyere is a pipe that directs air into the firepot to increase heat.

quiz.q: What is clinker?
options: B) A glassy waste that blocks air
quiz.explanation: Clinker is the glassy, rock-like waste from impurities in coal that can block air flow.

quiz.q: How long will a 9 kg propane cylinder typically run a small forge?
quiz.explanation: A 9 kg cylinder lasts about 8 to 10 hours at full blast.

quiz.q: What colour indicates a forging heat of about 1,100Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Orange corresponds to approximately 1,100Â°C, suitable for forging.

quiz.q: What should you do first if a coal fire gets too hot?
options: B) Turn off the air blast
quiz.explanation: Turning off the air blast reduces oxygen and cools the fire quickly.

quiz.q: Why should you never use petrol to start a forge fire?
options: C) It can cause a dangerous explosion
quiz.explanation: Petrol is highly volatile and can cause a flash fire or explosion.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to light a gas forge?
options: A) Open gas fully, then light
B) Light a match, then open gas
C) Open gas slightly, then light with a long lighter
quiz.explanation: Open the gas slightly, then light with a long lighter to avoid leaning over the forge.

quiz.q: What should you check for after connecting a gas hose?
options: B) Gas leaks with soapy water
C) Air bubbles in the hose
D) The colour of the hose
quiz.explanation: Soapy water will bubble if there is a gas leak, allowing you to tighten connections.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a gas forge flame needs more air?
options: A) It is blue and roaring
B) It is yellow and lazy
quiz.explanation: A yellow, lazy flame indicates incomplete combustion and needs more air.

quiz.q: How can you save gas when using a gas forge?
options: A) Leave it running all day
B) Turn down the burner when not heating metal
quiz.explanation: Turning down the burner when not in use reduces fuel consumption.

quiz.q: What is the first step in building a coal fire?
options: B) Place kindling in the bottom
C) Turn on the air blast fully
D) Pour water on the firepot
quiz.explanation: Start with kindling or paper at the bottom to ignite the fire.

quiz.q: What does green coal do when first added to the fire?
options: B) Smokes and gives off yellow smoke
quiz.explanation: Green coal smokes as it heats and turns to coke, which burns clean.

quiz.q: How deep should metal be placed in a coal fire?
options: A) On top of the coal
D) At the bottom of the firepot
quiz.explanation: Placing metal 2-3 cm below the surface ensures even heating in the hottest zone.

quiz.q: What is a common air supply tool for a charcoal forge in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Hand-powered bellows, often made from plastic bags or wooden boxes, are common and affordable.

quiz.q: What temperature is needed for forge welding?
quiz.explanation: Forge welding requires a white heat of about 1,300Â°C.

quiz.q: How can you decrease the temperature of a coal fire?
options: C) Reduce air or spread the coal
quiz.explanation: Reducing air or spreading the coal lowers the heat.

quiz.q: What is a damper used for on a forge?
options: B) To make fine adjustments to air supply
quiz.explanation: A damper controls the air flow, allowing precise temperature control.

quiz.q: Why is it important to control fire size?
options: A) To save fuel and heat metal efficiently
B) To make the fire look nice
quiz.explanation: Controlling fire size saves fuel and ensures efficient heating for different jobs.

quiz.q: What should you do before lighting a gas forge?
options: A) Check for leaks with soapy water
quiz.explanation: Checking for leaks prevents accidents and ensures safe operation.

quiz.q: What is the correct flame for a gas forge?
quiz.explanation: A blue, roaring flame indicates proper air-gas mixture and efficient combustion.

quiz.q: What should you do if you smell gas from a gas forge?
options: A) Light a match to find the leak
B) Turn off the cylinder and ventilate
quiz.explanation: Turn off the gas immediately and ventilate to avoid explosion or poisoning.

quiz.q: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous?
options: B) It is invisible and deadly
C) It makes the forge cold
quiz.explanation: Carbon monoxide is odourless, invisible, and can cause death if inhaled.

quiz.q: What should you keep near your forge for fire safety?
options: A) A bucket of water and sand
quiz.explanation: Water and sand are effective for extinguishing small fires.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do if a coal fire spreads to nearby materials?
options: D) Turn on the air blast
quiz.explanation: Water or sand can smother the flames and prevent spread.

quiz.q: How should you treat a minor burn?
options: B) Cool with running water for 10 minutes
quiz.explanation: Cooling with water reduces pain and prevents further tissue damage.

quiz.q: Why should you not pour water on a hot cast iron firepot?
options: B) It can crack the cast iron
D) It puts out the fire too quickly
quiz.explanation: Rapid cooling can cause cast iron to crack due to thermal shock.

quiz.q: What is the best way to clean a gas forge floor?
options: A) Use a wire brush or scraper
quiz.explanation: A wire brush or scraper removes scale and flux without damaging the lining.

quiz.q: How often should you check the gas hose and regulator?
quiz.explanation: Regular checks before each use prevent accidents from worn or cracked parts.
